Borrow the project budget now or draw it in stages? Follow debt, unused cash and carrying costs

Compare an immediate project-loan draw with three draws tied to bills, then reconcile interest, draw fees, interest on idle borrowed cash and the principal still owed.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare one immediate draw with three draws aligned to project bills

Interactive planning lab

Immediate draw: 12-month net carrying cost$4,350
Staged draws: 12-month net carrying cost$2,950
Staged cost less immediate-draw cost-$1,400

Original hypothetical 12-month comparison of two draw schedules on an assumed approved facility. Both finance the same three equal bills, due at the start of months spacing, twice spacing and three times spacing. One draws the entire project amount at time zero. The other draws only the bill amount at each due date, with all later draws assumed available. Rates stay fixed and annual rates divided by 12 apply to the post-bill balance for each whole monthly period. This deliberately simplified convention is not a reproduction of daily contractual interest. Borrowing interest and fees are paid from separate household cash; they are not capitalized. Interest on unused borrowed cash is paid out separately, before tax, and is not reinvested in the project pot. Neither alternative repays principal during the modeled year. Net carrying cost means borrowing interest plus draw fees less cash interest, not total project cost or total future repayment. Negative net cost can occur under entered rates and is not an available borrowing/deposit arrangement.

The central idea

Borrowed cash comes with matching debt. Aligning draws with bills can change carrying costs, but an undrawn limit is a different resource and the final project debt still needs repayment.

01

Separate the approved limit, the borrowing transaction and the project bill

A project budget can be known well before all of its bills are due. Borrowing the full amount immediately creates cash in an account, but it also creates debt immediately. Drawing only when a bill is due leaves less debt outstanding earlier, provided those later draws remain available under the actual arrangement.

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s line-of-credit explanation distinguishes a credit limit from money borrowed and explains that interest applies to drawn amounts. It also identifies possible fees and the consequence of paying interest without reducing principal. Those general mechanics provide the context for this illustration.

The model compares two schedules on an assumed facility, rather than two actual loan offers. Each finances the same CAD 60,000 project. One draws CAD 60,000 now; the other draws CAD 20,000 for each of three bills. Approval, continued access and payment of every bill are assumptions that require separate evidence in an actual plan.

02

Put the three bills at explicit points inside the year

The default bills arrive at the start of months three, six and nine. The first two monthly periods therefore pass before the first bill. Changing the spacing moves all three dates together while keeping their amounts equal. A spacing of four places the final bill at the start of month twelve.

The immediate-draw schedule owes CAD 60,000 throughout the year. Its borrowed project cash falls to CAD 40,000 at the first bill, CAD 20,000 at the second and zero at the third. Paying a contractor uses the cash; it does not repay the lender.

The staged schedule owes nothing in the first two monthly periods, CAD 20,000 in months three through five, CAD 40,000 in months six through eight, and CAD 60,000 in months nine through twelve. Every draw goes straight to the associated bill. Both schedules therefore finish with the same amount spent on the project and the same principal owed.

03

Charge interest to the debt that is actually outstanding

The default annual borrowing input is 8%, with one twelfth applied to each monthly period. The immediate schedule pays CAD 400 of interest per month and CAD 4,800 over twelve months. The staged schedule pays interest on its smaller early balances and pays CAD 2,800 over the same horizon.

This is a deliberately uniform monthly convention. FCAC describes interest running from withdrawal until repayment; actual agreements may calculate it daily and apply variable rates. The illustration holds its rates fixed and does not claim that each real calendar month has the same day count.

All borrowing interest is paid from separate household cash. It is not added to principal, funded by another draw or deducted from the cash earmarked for bills. That keeps the full project funded in both schedules, but it also means the household needs another budget line for those monthly payments. Counting the project loan as sufficient to cover both the bills and those separate interest payments would overstate the funds provided.

04

Include interest on unused borrowed cash without counting it twice

The immediate schedule holds borrowed money before the project needs it. At the hypothetical 2% annual cash-interest input, its unused project cash earns CAD 500 over the modeled year. The interest is paid out to separate household cash and is not compounded or used to change the project’s bill amounts.

The cash pot contains CAD 60,000 for two monthly periods, CAD 40,000 for three, and CAD 20,000 for three. Multiplying those balances by their periods and the monthly cash rate gives the CAD 500 amount. The staged schedule has no idle project cash because each draw immediately pays a bill.

The income offsets part of the immediate schedule’s borrowing cost, but it does not turn borrowed principal into new household wealth. At the initial draw, CAD 60,000 of cash and CAD 60,000 of debt arise together. The model also makes no assumption that project spending creates an asset worth its cost. Any market value, resale proceeds or tax treatment would need its own evidence.

05

Reconcile fees before describing the net saving

A hypothetical CAD 50 fee applies to each positive draw and is paid from household cash. The immediate schedule has one fee of CAD 50. The staged schedule has three fees totaling CAD 150. These are entered assumptions, rather than a claim about common lender pricing.

The immediate schedule’s net carrying cost is therefore CAD 4,800 of borrowing interest plus CAD 50 of fees minus CAD 500 of cash interest, or CAD 4,350. The staged schedule costs CAD 2,800 plus CAD 150, or CAD 2,950. Staged cost less immediate cost is negative CAD 1,400 under the default inputs.

The waterfall reconciles that signed difference. It adds staged interest and fees, subtracts the immediate schedule’s interest and fee, then adds back the income already deducted from the immediate cost. This last sign matters: ignoring the income would exaggerate the staged schedule’s advantage. No extra principal deduction belongs in the comparison because the same CAD 60,000 debt remains in both alternatives.

06

Test the bill dates and rates, then plan the debt repayment

The matrix replaces the borrowing rate and the bill spacing while holding project size, cash yield and draw fee selected. Later bills leave more borrowed money idle under the immediate schedule. A larger borrowing-rate margin over the cash rate increases that carrying-cost difference, while extra draw fees can offset it.

The cells are alternative calculations, not forecasts of rates or approval. An entered cash rate above the borrowing rate can even produce negative net carrying cost for the immediate schedule. That is a mathematical consequence of the assumptions, rather than evidence that such an arrangement is available, permitted or attractive after tax and other costs.

The final planning task remains principal repayment. The calculation stops after twelve months with the project paid and its debt outstanding. It does not assume a home sale, refinancing, future income increase or another loan will clear that balance. Keep the draw calendar, monthly carrying budget and eventual repayment source together. A lower first-year financing cost can improve the cash plan while leaving the same long-term debt obligation.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All four charts use original hypothetical draw schedules and fixed rates. FCAC supplies general line-of-credit context; the tool does not reproduce a lender’s daily-interest method, quote, approval criteria or facility agreement. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
